paragraphs.text: Even before we received the letter from your love, report had reached us of the purity of your faith: how it stands firm against dangers and endures the sufferings borne for Christ, and how your love for God and your hope of what is to come remain steadfast among you. And now that we have also read the letter of your piety, we have seen in it the true stamp of an apostolic church, the zeal of good shepherds, and a tireless earnestness fitting for genuine Christians. You took no account of the length of the journey, and you did not send your questions separately but put them together in a single letter. This has given us great hope that, having written in agreement, you will also receive our answers in agreement; and we have welcomed the harmony of your letter as a kind of prelude to a more complete harmony. It was indeed our prayer to receive the most admirable bishop Basil, a name spoken with all reverence, here in person at the synod, and to have him as our partner, or rather our leader, in the matters concerning you. But since a severe bodily illness prevented him from coming, it will be a mark of your perfect love not to disregard the letter of our own lowliness. Yet we have not allowed your holy church to go without his voice as well. We have a treatise of his composed specifically on this very subject, and so through his writing we have him speaking together with us.

What, then, is our answer to your question? We acknowledge the holy synod of the fathers at Nicaea as a truly catholic and apostolic synod, and we keep the faith set out by the fathers at that time unmoved and unshaken, and I pray that it may remain intact for ever. At that time it was more necessary for the fathers to explain at greater length the glory of the Only-begotten, since they were eager to cut down the heresy of Arius, which had only recently sprung up, destroying its first seeds before the thorn grew fully hardened. Since the question concerning the Spirit had not then been raised, they added nothing at greater length on it. Yet for those who read with understanding, the teaching about the Spirit in that creed is also sufficient. For just as they decreed that we believe in the Father and the Son, so they decreed that we believe in the Spirit, neither introducing any other nature into the divine and blessed Trinity nor cutting off anything belonging to the Trinity in their statement of the faith. But since Satan, trying to unsettle the churches, has recently cast doubt about the Spirit into some minds, it is necessary to go back to the source of the faith, from which the fathers at Nicaea also drew when they composed their statement of the faith.

What, then, is the fullness of our faith? It is the tradition of the Lord, which after his resurrection from the dead he committed to his holy disciples, commanding them: "Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." Clearly we have received this command not only to baptize in this way but also to make disciples in this way. Through this command the disease of Sabellius is shut out, since the three hypostases have been plainly handed down to us; and the mouths of the Anomoeans, the Arians and the Pneumatomachi are stopped, since three persons and three hypostases are made known while one nature and one Godhead are confessed. We must therefore baptize as we were taught, believe as we were baptized, and give glory as we have believed. For though we have examined the matter thoroughly in our minds and turned our reasoning in every direction, we can conceive of nothing between the Creator and the creation. So if we separate the Spirit from the Godhead, we must number it among the creatures; and if we dared to call it a creature, how could it be joined with the Father and the Son in baptism? We condemn polytheism just as we condemn atheism. We proclaim neither three first principles, nor three gods, nor three different natures; rather, while acknowledging the Father as the first principle of all things, we reject none of the three hypostases, and we bring forward the solemn witness of the divine Scriptures and their testimonies concerning each.

But to discuss these matters in fine detail goes beyond the limits of a letter, and we have trusted that your love will be satisfied with the main points of our statement and will supply the rest from your own resources, for Scripture says, "Give a wise man an opportunity, and he will become wiser." So we consider that what we have written is enough, and it remains only to add a brief exhortation. We urge you to remain children of peace, so that you may fulfil the apostle's command, being of one soul and one mind, as you have also shared in the sufferings endured for Christ. Do not let the evil one divide what is well joined together, and do not make yourselves easier prey for the wolves by your dissension, fulfilling their wishes. For we have learned how many struggles you have endured for the sake of orthodoxy. Having overcome the threats and compulsion of your opponents, give no opportunity to division, lest hatred, slipping in little by little, should gain a foothold and set great precipices beneath your feet. Rather, in the doxologies too you must glorify the Spirit together with the Father and the Son, and you must know this: those who commit the unforgivable sin through blasphemy against the Spirit refuse communion with the Arians in vain, for they will be condemned along with them. We pray that you will keep the body of the Church undivided and free from strife, that you may spend the rest of your time in this present age in peace, and that you may stand in glory before the judgment seat of Christ on the day of judgment.
